extracted.intended_audience: NLP/ML researchers, program chairs, and scientists interested in peer-review analysis and NLP applications using peer-review data
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and annotated-aspect definitions used for scoring conference paper reviews (ACL family) and the dataset construction/annotation rules used in PeerRead. Includes per-aspect 1–5 scales, presentation-format guidance, and dataset collection/labeling procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness (1-5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the paper fit in ACL 2016? (Please answer this question in light of the desire to broaden the scope of the research areas represented at ACL.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scale: 5 = Certainly; 4 = Probably; 3 = Unsure; 2 = Probably not; 1 = Certainly not. If reviewers do not explicitly address an aspect, use a special 'not discussed' value during annotation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity (1-5)
rubrics_metrics.description: For the reasonably well-prepared reader, is it clear what was done and why? Is the paper well-written and well-structured?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scale definitions: 5 = Very clear; 4 = Understandable by most readers; 3 = Mostly understandable to me with some effort; 2 = Important questions were hard to resolve even with effort; 1 = Much of the paper is confusing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality (1-5)
rubrics_metrics.description: How original is the approach? Does this paper break new ground in topic, methodology, or content? How exciting and innovative is the research it describes? (A paper could score high for originality even if results do not show convincing benefit.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scale: 5 = Surprising (significant new problem/technique/insight, no prior research attempted something similar); 4 = Creative; 3 = Respectable; 2 = Pedestrian; 1 = Significant portions have been done before or done better.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical Soundness / Correctness (1-5)
rubrics_metrics.description: First, is the technical approach sound and well-chosen? Second, can one trust the empirical claims of the paper -- are they supported by proper experiments and are the results correctly interpreted?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scale: 5 = approach apt and claims convincingly supported; 4 = generally solid though some doubts; 3 = fairly reasonable but not fully convincing; 2 = troublesome; 1 = fatally flawed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theoretical Soundness / Correctness (1-5)
rubrics_metrics.description: First, is the mathematical approach sound and well-chosen? Second, are the arguments in the paper cogent and well-supported?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scale mirrors empirical soundness: 5 = mathematical approach apt and claims convincingly supported; down to 1 = fatally flawed. Use to evaluate formal/theoretical work specifically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaningful Comparison (1-5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do the authors make clear where the problems and methods sit with respect to existing literature? Are the references adequate? For empirical papers, are the experimental results meaningfully compared with the best prior approaches?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scale: 5 = precise and complete comparison with related work; 4 = mostly solid but some references missing; 3 = somewhat helpful but could leave readers unsure how work relates to prior work; 2 = partial awareness or flawed empirical comparison; 1 = little awareness or necessary comparison missing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substance (1-5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Does this paper have enough substance, or would it benefit from more ideas or results? (This concerns amount of work rather than quality.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scale: 5 = contains more ideas/results than most publications (goes the extra mile); 4 = appropriate amount of work for the conference (most submissions); 3 = leaves one or two natural questions unpursued; 2 = work in progress; 1 = seems thin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact of ideas or results (1-5)
rubrics_metrics.description: How significant is the work described? If the ideas are novel, will they be useful or inspirational? Does the paper bring new insights into the nature of the problem?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scale: 5 = will affect the field by altering others' choices of research topics or basic approach; 4 = will substantially help others' ongoing research; 3 = interesting but not highly influential; 2 = marginally interesting; 1 = no impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact of accompanying software (1-5)
rubrics_metrics.description: If software was submitted or released with the paper, what is the expected impact of the software package? Will it be valuable to others or fill an unmet need? Is it at least sufficient to replicate or better understand the research?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scale: 5 = enabling (affects choices of research/development); 4 = useful (recommendable to others); 3 = potentially useful; 2 = documentary (useful to replicate but limited broader use); 1 = no usable software released.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact of accompanying dataset (1-5)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a dataset was submitted/released with the paper, what is the expected impact of the dataset? Will it be valuable to others in the form released? Does it fill an unmet need?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scale: 5 = enabling; 4 = useful; 3 = potentially useful; 2 = documentary; 1 = no usable dataset submitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation / Overall recommendation (1-5)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are many good submissions competing for slots; how important is it to feature this one? Will people learn a lot by reading or seeing it presented? Should the paper be accepted or rejected?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: In deciding, consider all aspect scores. Remember authors can address reviewer comments. Scale: 5 = changed my thinking; I'd fight to get it accepted; 4 = learned a lot and would like it accepted; 3 = borderline; 2 = leaning against; 1 = poor, would fight to reject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer Confidence (1-5)
rubrics_metrics.description: How confident is the reviewer that their evaluation is correct?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scale: 5 = positive (read carefully and familiar with related work); 4 = quite sure; 3 = pretty sure but might have missed something; 2 = fairly likely missed details; 1 = not my area or paper hard to understand (educated guess).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation format (oral vs poster) decision criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommendation whether an accepted submission should be an oral or poster presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Program-chair guidance: base this decision on the expected size of interested audience and whether the ideas can be grasped without back-and-forth discussion. Empirically, reviews recommending oral presentations have higher overall and aspect scores (e.g., substance, clarity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Aspect-score annotation procedure (dataset annotation rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Annotators annotated seven aspects per review: appropriateness, clarity, originality, soundness/correctness, meaningful comparison, substance, and impact; annotators used the ACL2016 instructions and read the review text only, selecting integer scores 1–5 or 'not discussed' if aspect absent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Annotation feasibility: annotators inferred about half of aspects from review text. Average absolute difference to gold where aspect discussed: 0.51 (1–5 scale). Re-annotation consistency: 77% consistent (same or off by 1), 2% off by ≥2 points; 21% disagreements where one marked 'not discussed'.

rubrics_metrics.name: arXiv labeling rules for accepted vs probably-rejected
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedure used to label arXiv submissions as 'accepted' or 'probably-rejected' relative to a group of target top-tier venues (ACL, EMNLP, NAACL, EACL, TACL, NIPS, ICML, ICLR, AAAI).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accepted: use Sutton & Gong (2017) matches DBLP bibliographic entries by comparing titles & author names (Jaccard distance); also add arXiv submission if title matches an accepted paper with relative Levenshtein distance < 0.1. Probably-rejected criteria: not accepted to any target venue; submitted to cs.cl, cs.lg or cs.ai; not cross-listed in non-cs categories; submission date within one month of target venue deadlines; submission date coincides with at least one arXiv paper accepted at a target venue. Data-quality checks included searching comments indicating 'accept' and manual inspection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review collection inclusion criteria (opt-in and web sources)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules for inclusion of reviewed papers in PeerRead from various sources: opted-in (Softconf opt-in for CoNLL2016, ACL2017), NIPS public reviews (accepted papers only), OpenReview (ICLR official reviews).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opted-in inclusion: a submission included only if (i) corresponding author opts-in the paper draft, and (ii) at least one reviewer opts-in their anonymous review. Opted-in reviews include text and aspect scores (1–5). OpenReview and NIPS sections include official anonymous reviews (NIPS only for accepted papers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Features correlated with acceptance (used for automated acceptance prediction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hand-engineered features found predictive of acceptance in the paper-acceptance classification experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most salient: presence of appendix; large number of theorems/equations; average length of text preceding a citation (avg_len_ref); number of recent references (within five years); whether abstract contains 'state_of_the_art' (ICLR) or 'neural' (arXiv); title length; number of unique words. Ablation showed removing appendix or num_theorems caused largest accuracy drops on ICLR/ICLR-like data. These are predictive correlations (not normative guidelines).
